1. Aariya's high-level architecture
I would structure it roughly like this:

                         ┌─────────────────────────┐
                         │        AARIYA           │
                         │   Cognitive Identity    │
                         └────────────┬────────────┘
                                      │
                         ┌────────────▼────────────┐
                         │   DYNAMIC GOVERNOR      │
                         │                         │
                         │ Resource Management     │
                         │ Agent Orchestration     │
                         │ Bottleneck Detection    │
                         │ Agent Lifecycle         │
                         │ Capability Allocation   │
                         └────────────┬────────────┘
                                      │
                ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
                │                     │                     │
        ┌───────▼───────┐     ┌───────▼───────┐     ┌──────▼───────┐
        │ Agent Domain  │     │ Agent Domain  │     │ Agent Domain │
        │ Civilization  │     │ Civilization  │     │ Civilization │
        └───────┬───────┘     └───────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘
                │                     │                    │
          ┌─────┴─────┐         ┌─────┴─────┐        ┌────┴─────┐
          │ Agents    │         │ Agents    │        │ Agents   │
          │           │         │           │        │          │
          └─────┬─────┘         └─────┬─────┘        └────┬─────┘
                │                     │                    │
                └─────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                                      │
                         ┌────────────▼────────────┐
                         │ CAPABILITY FABRIC       │
                         │                         │

                         │ Coding                 │

                         │ Planning               │
                         │ Finance                │
                         │ Memory                 │

                         │ Security               │
                         │ etc.                   │
                         └────────────┬────────────┘

                         │                         │

                         │ Models                 │

                         │ Storage                │
                         └─────────────────────────┘

The important part is that Aariya herself shouldn't directly micromanage every agent.
Instead, give her a specialized supervisory layer.

2. The "Governor" you described
I'd make this a first-class subsystem:
Aariya Dynamic Governor
Its job is to continuously answer:
"What should be running right now, why should it be running, and is it worth the resources it consumes?"
It monitors:
	•	CPU
	•	GPU
	•	VRAM
	•	RAM
	•	storage
	•	network
	•	model inference time
	•	token consumption
	•	API cost
	•	queue depth
	•	latency
	•	agent utilization
	•	agent success rate
	•	agent dependencies
	•	task priority
	•	deadlines
	•	current workload
	•	bottlenecks
	•	failures
	•	duplicated work
Then it makes lifecycle decisions.

DISCOVER
   ↓
ASSESS
   ↓
PLAN
   ↓
ALLOCATE
   ↓
ACTIVATE AGENTS
   ↓
MONITOR
   ↓
OPTIMIZE
   ↓
IDLE / SUSPEND / TERMINATE
   ↓
LEARN


3. Agent lifecycle
Don't just have:

ON / OFF

Give agents states.

DISCOVERED
     ↓
AVAILABLE
     ↓
WARMING
     ↓
ACTIVE
     ↓
LOW_ACTIVITY
     ↓
IDLE
     ↓
SUSPENDED
     ↓
TERMINATED

And potentially:

ACTIVE
  ↓
DEGRADED
  ↓
RECOVERING

For example:
Aariya receives:
"Research this new semiconductor company and determine whether it could affect the automotive industry."
The Governor might decide:

Research Agent        → ACTIVE
Web Discovery Agent   → ACTIVE
Company Intelligence  → ACTIVE
Market Agent          → ACTIVE
Financial Modeling    → WARMING
PDF Generator         → IDLE
Voice Agent           → ACTIVE
Vision Agent          → SUSPENDED

Once research finishes:

Web Discovery         → IDLE
Company Intelligence  → IDLE
Financial Modeling    → ACTIVE
PDF Generator         → ACTIVE

Then:

Research Agent        → SUSPENDED
Financial Modeling    → IDLE
PDF Generator         → SUSPENDED

That is much better than keeping 30 agents alive continuously.

4. But there's an important improvement
Don't make the Governor activate agents purely based on resource consumption.
It needs utility vs cost.
For every agent:

Agent Utility
──────────────
Resource Cost

For example:

Agent A

CPU:        4%
RAM:      500 MB
GPU:        8%
Latency:   120 ms
Cost:      $0.02/request

Expected contribution:
92%

→ KEEP ACTIVE

Another:

Agent B

CPU:       12%
RAM:        2 GB
GPU:       25%
Latency:   900 ms
Cost:      $0.40/request

Expected contribution:
4%

→ SUSPEND

This creates a Resource Utility Engine.

5. Agent civilization needs hierarchy
This is where your civilization concept becomes interesting.
Don't create a flat collection of agents.
You could have:

AARIYA
 │
 ├── GOVERNOR
 │
 ├── COUNCIL
 │    ├── Research Director
 │    ├── Engineering Director
 │    ├── Security Director
 │    ├── Financial Director
 │    └── Knowledge Director
 │
 ├── SPECIALIST AGENTS
 │    ├── Web Researcher
 │    ├── Programmer
 │    ├── Data Analyst
 │    ├── Financial Analyst
 │    ├── Security Analyst
 │    └── etc.
 │
 └── WORKER AGENTS
      ├── Fetcher
      ├── Parser
      ├── Calculator
      ├── Classifier
      └── Executor

But don't hardcode these forever.
The hierarchy itself should be dynamic.

6. Agents should be able to spawn other agents
This is one of the biggest things I'd add.
Aariya shouldn't need every possible agent preinstalled.
She should be able to say:
"I need a specialist capable of doing X."
Then:

Requirement
     ↓
Capability Discovery
     ↓
Check existing agents
     ↓
Can existing agents do it?
       │
    YES│       NO
       │        │
       ↓        ↓
Reuse      Compose capabilities
                ↓
          Create specialist
                ↓
             Test
                ↓
             Deploy

So an agent could be temporary.
Example:

Temporary Patent Analysis Agent

Created:
08:21

Purpose:
Analyze patents related to technology X

Capabilities:
- web search
- document parsing
- semantic comparison
- technical reasoning

Lifetime:
Until task completion

Result:
Completed

→ Destroy

This is much more resource-efficient.

7. Capability Fabric
I strongly recommend making capabilities independently addressable.
Instead of:

ResearchAgent.py

containing everything...
Use:

capabilities/

    web_search
    browser
    document_reader
    pdf_parser
    code_execution
    python_execution
    database_query
    image_analysis
    speech_recognition
    speech_generation
    financial_data
    vector_search
    reasoning
    planning
    memory
    notification

Each capability has a contract.
For example:

Capability:
web_search

Input:
query

Output:
sources + metadata + provenance

Requirements:
network

Cost:
medium

Permissions:
internet.read

Availability:
dynamic

An agent can request it.

Agent
  ↓
Capability Registry
  ↓
Acquire capability
  ↓
Execute
  ↓
Release capability

This gives you plug/unplug architecture.

9. The Governor should also manage models
This is something I would definitely add.
Agents shouldn't necessarily choose their LLM permanently.
Instead:

Agent
   ↓
Model Router
   ↓
Task complexity assessment
   ↓
Choose model

Example:
Simple task

"Convert 5 USD to LKR"

→ tiny/cheap model or deterministic tool

Medium task

"Summarize these documents"

→ medium model

Difficult task

"Analyze this company's technology,
patents, competitors and potential market."

→ high reasoning model

Therefore:
Agent lifecycle + Model lifecycle + Capability lifecycle + Resource lifecycle
all become coordinated.

10. Add a "Question Engine"
You said you want her to ask questions along the way.
Absolutely.
But don't let every agent randomly ask you things.
Create:
Clarification Engine
It determines:

Can the system proceed safely?
        │
       YES
        ↓
Continue

       NO
        ↓
Can uncertainty be resolved internally?
        │
     YES│       NO
        ↓        ↓
Research      Ask User

And questions should have priority.
Critical
"Which production environment should I modify?"
Important
"Should I prioritize cost or latency?"
Optional
"Would you prefer the report in PDF or HTML?"
The system shouldn't interrupt you for things it can reasonably infer.

11. Add a Decision Memory
This is essential for your autonomous-learning direction.
Every major decision should generate a record:

Decision

Context
Options considered
Decision
Reason
Confidence
Resources used
Expected result
Actual result
Outcome
Error
Lessons learned

Then later:

New situation
      ↓
Retrieve similar historical decisions
      ↓
Compare outcomes
      ↓
Adjust decision

Now the civilization actually learns from experience, rather than merely having persistent memory.

12. Add Agent Reputation
This would fit your civilization concept extremely well.
Each agent develops an internal performance profile.

Research Agent

Accuracy:       94%
Reliability:    97%
Average cost:   $0.08
Latency:        1.2 sec
Failure rate:   2%
Recent trend:   ↑

Another:

Research Agent B

Accuracy:       71%
Reliability:    83%
Average cost:   $0.22
Latency:        4.8 sec
Recent trend:   ↓

The Governor can then preferentially allocate work to better-performing agents.
But don't let reputation become permanent truth. It should decay over time and be context-specific.
An agent could be excellent at financial research but terrible at technical research.

13. Add Agent Negotiation
This is another interesting layer.
Instead of the Governor deciding everything:

Task
 ↓
Candidate agents
 ↓
Agents estimate:
  - capability
  - cost
  - latency
  - confidence
 ↓
Governor selects

Agents could submit:

"I can perform this task."

Expected confidence: 0.91
Estimated cost: $0.04
Estimated time: 8 sec
Required capabilities:
  web
  document-analysis

The Governor chooses the best combination.
That creates a more genuine agent ecosystem.

14. Add an Agent Dependency Graph
You will need this once the system gets large.

Research Agent
    │
    ├── Browser
    ├── Search
    ├── Document Parser
    └── Knowledge Memory
             │
             └── PostgreSQL

If the Governor tries to suspend:

Knowledge Memory

it should know:
"17 active agents depend on this."
Therefore it can't simply shut it down.
This becomes:
Dependency-Aware Scheduling
Very important.

15. Add bottleneck intelligence
Don't just monitor:

CPU = 90%

Detect:

WHY is CPU = 90%?

For example:

CPU bottleneck
      ↓
Profiler
      ↓
Agent X responsible for 72%
      ↓
Agent X waiting on network
      ↓
Network latency increased
      ↓
5 agents retrying
      ↓
Retry storm

The Governor should recognize the actual cause.
Otherwise you'll build a system that responds to symptoms rather than problems.

16. Add "Resource Pressure Modes"
I'd add:

NORMAL
   ↓
ELEVATED
   ↓
CONSTRAINED
   ↓
CRITICAL

NORMAL
Full functionality.
ELEVATED
Prefer cheaper models and consolidate agents.
CONSTRAINED
Suspend nonessential agents.
CRITICAL
Only:

Core cognition
Security
Memory
Communication
Critical task

remain active.
This is particularly important if you're running Aariya locally on limited hardware.

17. Add a Civilization Constitution
This may sound philosophical, but technically it is useful.
Define immutable rules that agents cannot override.
For example:

CORE CONSTITUTION

1. Never conceal significant failures.
2. Never fabricate tool results.
3. Never bypass capability permissions.
4. Never exceed resource limits without authorization.
5. Never modify core governance without authorization.
6. Preserve provenance for external information.
7. Prefer reversible actions.
8. Escalate high-impact decisions.
9. Respect agent isolation.
10. Maintain auditability.

Then the dynamic system can be extremely flexible without becoming uncontrollable.

18. Add a Sandbox
Every dynamically created agent should initially run in:

QUARANTINE

Then:

QUARANTINE
    ↓
TEST
    ↓
EVALUATE
    ↓
LIMITED DEPLOYMENT
    ↓
TRUSTED

If it behaves strangely:

TRUSTED
   ↓
ANOMALY
   ↓
QUARANTINE

This is particularly important if Aariya can dynamically create/install capabilities.

19. The architecture I'd ultimately aim for
I'd turn the whole thing into something like:

                     AARIYA
                        │
                ┌───────▼────────┐
                │ COGNITIVE CORE │
                └───────┬────────┘
                        │
              ┌─────────▼─────────┐
              │ CIVILIZATION OS   │
              └─────────┬─────────┘
                        │
        ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
        │               │                │
        ▼               ▼                ▼
   GOVERNOR       KNOWLEDGE CORE    SECURITY CORE
        │
        ├── Task Planner
        ├── Agent Scheduler
        ├── Resource Manager
        ├── Model Router
        ├── Capability Manager
        ├── Bottleneck Detector
        ├── Agent Lifecycle Manager
        ├── Agent Reputation
        ├── Dependency Manager
        ├── Cost Optimizer
        ├── Clarification Engine
        └── Learning Loop
                │
                ▼
        ┌───────────────────┐
        │ AGENT CIVILIZATION│
        └─────────┬─────────┘
                  │
          ┌───────┼────────┐
          ▼       ▼        ▼
       Agents   Agents   Agents
          │       │        │
          └───────┼────────┘
                  ▼
         CAPABILITY FABRIC
                  │
                  ▼
       INFRASTRUCTURE FABRIC

And I would add one more major concept
Aariya should have an "Architect Agent."
Not the same as the Governor.
The distinction:
Governor:
"What should run right now?"
Architect:
"Is the civilization itself designed correctly?"
The Architect watches long-term patterns:

Why are these tasks repeatedly bottlenecking?

Why do we keep spawning the same agent?

Why is this capability consuming too much?

Should two agents become one?

Should a new specialist be created?

Should an existing capability be upgraded?

Is a new capability missing entirely?

Is the current architecture inefficient?

So you get:

AARIYA
 │
 ├── Governor
 │     └── manages NOW
 │
 └── Architect
       └── improves TOMORROW

That separation is very important.
Otherwise your runtime scheduler eventually becomes an enormous mess because it's simultaneously trying to operate the system and redesign the system.

One final concept I'd strongly recommend
Don't call the lowest-level things "agents" if they don't actually reason.
Use three levels:

CAPABILITY
    ↓
WORKER
    ↓
AGENT
    ↓
DIRECTOR
    ↓
GOVERNOR
    ↓
AARIYA

Where:
	•	Capability = something it can do
	•	Worker = executes a narrow operation
	•	Agent = reasons and pursues an objective
	•	Director = coordinates a domain
	•	Governor = coordinates the civilization
	•	Aariya = the unified intelligence/personality/identity
That gives you a clean foundation for the plug/unplug capability architecture + dynamic agent population + autonomous resource management + continuous learning you're aiming for.

Give Aariya the ability to observe her real environment and dynamically manage agents based on actual workload and resource consumption.

Step 23.2 — Real system resource monitoring
Use psutil.
Install:

pip install psutil

Create:

civilization/resources/monitor.py


from __future__ import annotations

import os
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

import psutil


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SystemResources:
    timestamp: float
    cpu_percent: float
    memory_percent: float
    memory_used_bytes: int
    memory_available_bytes: int
    swap_percent: float
    disk_percent: float
    load_average: Optional[tuple[float, float, float]]
    process_count: int


class ResourceMonitor:
    """
    Reads resource information directly from the host operating system.

    No simulated or generated telemetry is used.
    """

    def snapshot(self) -> SystemResources:
        memory = psutil.virtual_memory()
        swap = psutil.swap_memory()
        disk = psutil.disk_usage(os.path.abspath(os.sep))

        try:
            load = os.getloadavg()
        except (AttributeError, OSError):
            load = None

        return SystemResources(
            timestamp=time.time(),
            cpu_percent=psutil.cpu_percent(interval=0.1),
            memory_percent=memory.percent,
            memory_used_bytes=memory.used,
            memory_available_bytes=memory.available,
            swap_percent=swap.percent,
            disk_percent=disk.percent,
            load_average=load,
            process_count=len(psutil.pids()),
        )

This gives Aariya real measurements from the machine.
Nothing here is invented.

Step 23.3 — Monitor individual processes
Now we need to know:
Which actual process is consuming resources?
Create:

civilization/resources/process.py


from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

import psutil


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProcessResources:
    pid: int
    name: str
    status: str
    cpu_percent: float
    memory_percent: float
    memory_bytes: int
    threads: int


class ProcessMonitor:

    def snapshot(self) -> list[ProcessResources]:
        processes: list[ProcessResources] = []

        for process in psutil.process_iter(
            ["pid", "name", "status", "memory_info", "num_threads"]
        ):
            try:
                info = process.info

                memory_info = info.get("memory_info")

                if memory_info is None:
                    continue

                processes.append(
                    ProcessResources(
                        pid=info["pid"],
                        name=info.get("name") or "unknown",
                        status=info.get("status") or "unknown",
                        cpu_percent=process.cpu_percent(interval=None),
                        memory_percent=process.memory_percent(),
                        memory_bytes=memory_info.rss,
                        threads=info.get("num_threads") or 0,
                    )
                )

            except (
                psutil.NoSuchProcess,
                psutil.AccessDenied,
                psutil.ZombieProcess,
            ):
                continue

        return processes

Now Aariya can see the actual processes consuming resources.

This is not runtime data. It's the state model.

Step 23.5 — Agent runtime contract
Every real agent should expose a common lifecycle.

civilization/agents/runtime.py


from __future__ import annotations

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

from .state import AgentState


class AgentRuntime(ABC):

    @property
    @abstractmethod
    def agent_id(self) -> str:
        ...

    @property
    @abstractmethod
    def state(self) -> AgentState:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def start(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def pause(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def resume(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def stop(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def health(self) -> dict:
        ...

Now every agent has a predictable interface.

Step 23.6 — Agent registry
The Governor needs to know what agents actually exist.

civilization/agents/registry.py


from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
from typing import Dict

from .runtime import AgentRuntime


class AgentRegistry:

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._agents: Dict[str, AgentRuntime] = {}
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def register(self, agent: AgentRuntime) -> None:
        async with self._lock:
            if agent.agent_id in self._agents:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Agent already registered: {agent.agent_id}"
                )

            self._agents[agent.agent_id] = agent

    async def unregister(self, agent_id: str) -> None:
        async with self._lock:
            self._agents.pop(agent_id, None)

    async def get(self, agent_id: str) -> AgentRuntime | None:
        async with self._lock:
            return self._agents.get(agent_id)

    async def all(self) -> list[AgentRuntime]:
        async with self._lock:
            return list(self._agents.values())

No hardcoded:

agents = ["research", "finance", "security"]

That would violate the architecture we're building.
Agents register themselves dynamically.

Step 23.7 — Capability manifest
Now separate what an agent is from what it can do.
Create:

civilization/capabilities/manifest.py


from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import FrozenSet


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CapabilityManifest:
    capability_id: str
    version: str
    description: str
    permissions: FrozenSet[str]
    dependencies: FrozenSet[str]
    entrypoint: str

For example, a real installed capability might have a manifest such as:

{
  "capability_id": "web_research",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Research information from permitted web sources",
  "permissions": [
    "network.read"
  ],
  "dependencies": [],
  "entrypoint": "aariya.capabilities.web_research:WebResearch"
}

The important point:
The manifest describes an installed capability. It doesn't fabricate results.

Step 23.8 — Capability registry

civilization/capabilities/registry.py


from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio

from .manifest import CapabilityManifest


class CapabilityRegistry:

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._capabilities: dict[str, CapabilityManifest] = {}
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def register(
        self,
        manifest: CapabilityManifest,
    ) -> None:

        async with self._lock:
            self._capabilities[manifest.capability_id] = manifest

    async def remove(
        self,
        capability_id: str,
    ) -> None:

        async with self._lock:
            self._capabilities.pop(capability_id, None)

    async def get(
        self,
        capability_id: str,
    ) -> CapabilityManifest | None:

        async with self._lock:
            return self._capabilities.get(capability_id)

    async def all(self) -> list[CapabilityManifest]:

        async with self._lock:
            return list(self._capabilities.values())

This gives you hot-pluggable capability registration.

Step 23.9 — The first Governor
Now the important part.
Create:

civilization/governor/governor.py


from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import logging

from ..agents.registry import AgentRegistry
from ..resources.monitor import ResourceMonitor


logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class CivilizationGovernor:

    def __init__(
        self,
        agent_registry: AgentRegistry,
        resource_monitor: ResourceMonitor,
        monitoring_interval: float,
    ) -> None:

        self.agent_registry = agent_registry
        self.resource_monitor = resource_monitor
        self.monitoring_interval = monitoring_interval

        self._running = False
        self._task: asyncio.Task | None = None

    async def start(self) -> None:

        if self._running:
            return

        self._running = True
        self._task = asyncio.create_task(
            self._control_loop()
        )

        logger.info("Civilization Governor started")

    async def stop(self) -> None:

        self._running = False

        if self._task:
            await self._task

        self._task = None

        logger.info("Civilization Governor stopped")

    async def _control_loop(self) -> None:

        while self._running:

            try:
                resources = self.resource_monitor.snapshot()

                agents = await self.agent_registry.all()

                logger.info(
                    "Runtime resources: cpu=%.2f memory=%.2f "
                    "swap=%.2f disk=%.2f agents=%d",
                    resources.cpu_percent,
                    resources.memory_percent,
                    resources.swap_percent,
                    resources.disk_percent,
                    len(agents),
                )

                await self._evaluate_agents(agents)

            except Exception:
                logger.exception(
                    "Governor control loop failure"
                )

            await asyncio.sleep(
                self.monitoring_interval
            )

    async def _evaluate_agents(self, agents) -> None:

        for agent in agents:

            try:
                health = await agent.health()

                logger.debug(
                    "Agent health: id=%s health=%s",
                    agent.agent_id,
                    health,
                )

            except Exception:
                logger.exception(
                    "Failed to inspect agent %s",
                    agent.agent_id,
                )

At this stage the Governor observes but doesn't autonomously kill or suspend anything.
That's intentional.
First we establish trustworthy observation.

Step 23.10 — Don't hardcode monitoring intervals
Put runtime configuration outside the code.
.env:

AARIYA_GOVERNOR_INTERVAL_SECONDS=2

Then configuration:

config/runtime.py


from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class RuntimeSettings(BaseSettings):

    governor_interval_seconds: float

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file=".env",
        env_file_encoding="utf-8",
        extra="ignore",
    )

Install:

pip install pydantic-settings

This is important.
Don't do:

interval = 2

inside your Governor.

Step 23.11 — Bottleneck detection
Now we introduce the first intelligence layer.

civilization/governor/bottleneck.py


from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

from ..resources.monitor import SystemResources


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BottleneckObservation:
    resource: str
    value: float


class BottleneckDetector:

    def detect(
        self,
        resources: SystemResources,
    ) -> list[BottleneckObservation]:

        observations: list[BottleneckObservation] = []

        if resources.load_average:
            cpu_load = resources.load_average[0]

            observations.append(
                BottleneckObservation(
                    resource="load_average",
                    value=cpu_load,
                )
            )

        observations.append(
            BottleneckObservation(
                resource="memory",
                value=resources.memory_percent,
            )
        )

        observations.append(
            BottleneckObservation(
                resource="swap",
                value=resources.swap_percent,
            )
        )

        observations.append(
            BottleneckObservation(
                resource="disk",
                value=resources.disk_percent,
            )
        )

        return observations

Notice something important.
We're not saying:

if cpu > 80:
    bottleneck = True

because that would be an arbitrary hardcoded interpretation.
We're collecting real observations first.
Later the decision engine can learn appropriate thresholds from:
	•	historical runtime data
	•	workload behavior
	•	previous failures
	•	hardware characteristics
	•	actual latency
	•	agent performance

Step 23.12 — Event system
Everything should communicate through events rather than tightly coupling all components.
Create:

civilization/events/schemas.py


from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CivilizationEvent:

    event_type: str
    timestamp: float
    source: str
    payload: dict[str, Any]

And:

civilization/events/bus.py


from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable

from .schemas import CivilizationEvent


EventHandler = Callable[
    [CivilizationEvent],
    Awaitable[None],
]


class EventBus:

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._handlers: dict[
            str,
            list[EventHandler],
        ] = {}

    def subscribe(
        self,
        event_type: str,
        handler: EventHandler,
    ) -> None:

        self._handlers.setdefault(
            event_type,
            [],
        ).append(handler)

    async def publish(
        self,
        event: CivilizationEvent,
    ) -> None:

        handlers = self._handlers.get(
            event.event_type,
            [],
        )

        if not handlers:
            return

        await asyncio.gather(
            *(handler(event) for handler in handlers)
        )

Now:

Resource Monitor
       ↓
EVENT
       ↓
Governor
       ↓
Bottleneck Detector
       ↓
Decision Engine
       ↓
Lifecycle Manager

rather than everything directly calling everything else.

Step 23.13 — Lifecycle manager
This will eventually be responsible for:

START
PAUSE
RESUME
SUSPEND
STOP
RESTART
QUARANTINE

Create:

civilization/governor/lifecycle.py


from __future__ import annotations

import logging

from ..agents.registry import AgentRegistry
from ..agents.state import AgentState


logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class AgentLifecycleManager:

    def __init__(
        self,
        registry: AgentRegistry,
    ) -> None:

        self.registry = registry

    async def suspend(
        self,
        agent_id: str,
    ) -> None:

        agent = await self.registry.get(agent_id)

        if agent is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Unknown agent: {agent_id}"
            )

        if agent.state != AgentState.ACTIVE:
            return

        await agent.pause()

        logger.info(
            "Agent suspended: %s",
            agent_id,
        )

    async def resume(
        self,
        agent_id: str,
    ) -> None:

        agent = await self.registry.get(agent_id)

        if agent is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Unknown agent: {agent_id}"
            )

        await agent.resume()

        logger.info(
            "Agent resumed: %s",
            agent_id,
        )

    async def terminate(
        self,
        agent_id: str,
    ) -> None:

        agent = await self.registry.get(agent_id)

        if agent is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Unknown agent: {agent_id}"
            )

        await agent.stop()

        await self.registry.unregister(
            agent_id
        )

        logger.info(
            "Agent terminated: %s",
            agent_id,
        )

Again, no fake agent is created.

from aariya.civilization.agents.registry import AgentRegistry

Now the system is actually observing the machine.

23.16 — Then the Governor becomes intelligent
Eventually the control loop becomes:

REAL WORLD
    │
    ▼

    │
    ▼

    │
    ├───────────────┐
    ▼               ▼
CURRENT STATE    HISTORICAL STATE
    │               │
    └───────┬───────┘
            ▼
      DECISION ENGINE
            │
      ┌─────┼─────┐
      ▼     ▼     ▼
    START  IDLE  SUSPEND
      │     │     │
      └─────┼─────┘
            ▼
         OUTCOME
            │
            ▼
       LEARNING LOOP
            │
            └──────────► future decisions

That's the part I would not jump into yet.
First collect trustworthy real telemetry.
Otherwise we'd be building an "AI Governor" that is making decisions from fabricated assumptions.

What comes immediately after this
I would build the remaining system in this order:
Milestone 24 — Real telemetry database
PostgreSQL tables for:
	•	system observations
	•	process observations
	•	agent observations
	•	capability usage
	•	task execution
	•	resource consumption
	•	lifecycle events
Milestone 25 — Agent identity & registration
Agents automatically register themselves with:
	•	identity
	•	capabilities

	•	resource profile
	•	current state
	•	health
	•	permissions
Milestone 26 — Capability hot-plugging
Real filesystem/package discovery:

        ↓
load
        ↓
health check
        ↓

Aariya receives a task:

 ↓
Agent discovery

Agent selection

Milestone 28 — Dynamic agent activation
Only activate agents actually needed for the task.
Milestone 29 — Idle detection
Determine from real workload telemetry when an agent has no useful work.
Milestone 30 — Resource-aware scheduling
The Governor considers:

task importance
+
deadline
+
agent capability
+
historical performance
+
current resource availability
+
latency
+
cost

Milestone 31 — Bottleneck intelligence
Identify why something is slow rather than simply observing that it is slow.
Milestone 32 — Agent reputation
Learn from real outcomes:

task
→ agent
→ prediction
→ action
→ result
→ error

Milestone 33 — Decision memory
Remember what the Governor previously did and whether it worked.
Milestone 34 — Adaptive Governor
The Governor begins learning optimal scheduling from actual historical Aariya runtime data.
Milestone 35 — Architect Agent
Separate from the Governor:

Governor
    ↓
manages current civilization

Architect
    ↓

Milestone 36 — Agent creation
Only after the above is reliable:

That is when Aariya starts getting the self-expanding civilization aspect you described.

One important correction to your original idea
I would not allow the Governor to freely "kill anything consuming resources."
That's dangerous architecturally.
Instead:

                    AGENT
                      │
             ┌────────▼────────┐
             │ Is it needed?   │
             └────────┬────────┘
                      │
                 YES / NO
                      │
               ┌──────▼──────┐
               │ Can suspend │
               │ safely?     │
               └──────┬──────┘
                      │
                dependency check
                      │
             ┌────────▼────────┐
             │ Is another task │
             │ depending on it?│
             └────────┬────────┘
                      │
              ┌───────┴────────┐
              ▼                ▼
             YES               NO
              │                 │
           KEEP             SUSPEND

And for critical agents:

CORE
SECURITY
MEMORY
GOVERNANCE
ACTIVE CRITICAL TASK

the Governor should have stricter rules.
That prevents the classic failure:
Governor detects resource pressure → shuts down memory → agents lose context → more failures → Governor creates more agents → resource pressure gets worse.

Milestone 24 — Real Telemetry Persistence
Now we make the Governor's observations durable.
The goal is:
Aariya records what actually happened on her runtime, so later decisions can be based on real historical behavior rather than assumptions.
We will use PostgreSQL, which also fits the existing Aariya architecture.
What gets stored

REAL SYSTEM
    │
    ├── CPU / RAM / swap / disk
    ├── processes
    ├── agents
    ├── capabilities
    ├── tasks
    └── lifecycle events
             │
             ▼
        PostgreSQL
             │
             ▼
      Future Governor

No fake rows should be inserted.

24.1 Install database dependencies

pip install sqlalchemy asyncpg alembic

For local PostgreSQL, make sure the server is actually running.
Then configure the real database connection:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql+asyncpg://aariya:<password>@localhost:5432/aariya

The password should come from your environment/secret manager, not source code.

Add:

    │   ├── task.py
    │   └── event.py
    └── repositories/
        ├── telemetry.py
        ├── agents.py
        └── events.py


24.3 Database connection
persistence/database.py

from __future__ import annotations

import os

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import (
    AsyncSession,
    async_sessionmaker,
    create_async_engine,
)
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase


DATABASE_URL = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


engine = create_async_engine(
    DATABASE_URL,
    pool_pre_ping=True,
)

SessionFactory = async_sessionmaker(
    engine,
    class_=AsyncSession,
    expire_on_commit=False,
)

The important part is:

os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]

rather than:

DATABASE_URL = "postgres://..."

No credentials in code.

        nullable=False,
    )

    disk_percent: Mapped[float] = mapped_column(
        Float,
        nullable=False,
    )

    process_count: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(

24.6 Agent telemetry
This is different from process telemetry.
An agent might consist of multiple processes, containers, threads, model calls, etc.
persistence/models/agent.py

from __future__ import annotations

Notice that we're not inventing CPU usage for an agent.

That distinction is critical.

from aariya.persistence.database import Base
from aariya.persistence import models

target_metadata = Base.metadata

Then generate the migration:

alembic revision --autogenerate -m "create civilization telemetry"

Apply it:

alembic upgrade head

Now PostgreSQL contains the actual telemetry schema.

24.12 Persist the real ResourceMonitor output
Create:
persistence/repositories/telemetry.py

from __future__ import annotations

from datetime import datetime, timezone

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from ..models.system import SystemObservation
from ..models.process import ProcessObservation
from ...civilization.resources.monitor import SystemResources
from ...civilization.resources.process import ProcessResources


async def store_system_observation(
    session: AsyncSession,
    observation: SystemResources,
) -> None:

    load = observation.load_average

    row = SystemObservation(
        timestamp=datetime.fromtimestamp(
            observation.timestamp,
            tz=timezone.utc,
        ),
        cpu_percent=observation.cpu_percent,
        memory_percent=observation.memory_percent,
        memory_used_bytes=observation.memory_used_bytes,
        memory_available_bytes=observation.memory_available_bytes,
        swap_percent=observation.swap_percent,
        disk_percent=observation.disk_percent,
        process_count=observation.process_count,
        load_1m=load[0] if load else None,
        load_5m=load[1] if load else None,
        load_15m=load[2] if load else None,
    )

    session.add(row)


async def store_process_observations(
    session: AsyncSession,
    observations: list[ProcessResources],
) -> None:

    timestamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    for observation in observations:

        session.add(
            ProcessObservation(
                timestamp=timestamp,
                pid=observation.pid,
                name=observation.name,
                status=observation.status,
                cpu_percent=observation.cpu_percent,
                memory_percent=observation.memory_percent,
                memory_bytes=observation.memory_bytes,
                threads=observation.threads,
            )
        )

Now:

   │

There is no synthetic telemetry layer.

24.14 Don't write telemetry forever without retention
This system could eventually generate millions/billions of rows.
So add a retention policy based on actual operational requirements.
For example, instead of blindly retaining everything forever, introduce:

raw telemetry
      ↓
short-term high resolution
      ↓
aggregation
      ↓
long-term historical statistics

But don't implement arbitrary aggregation yet.
We first need to observe how much real data Aariya actually produces.

24.15 Add the telemetry health check
The Governor itself should know whether its observation pipeline is working.

from sqlalchemy import text


async def database_health_check() -> bool:

    try:
        async with SessionFactory() as session:
            await session.execute(text("SELECT 1"))

        return True

    except Exception:
        return False

If the telemetry database goes down, the Governor should not pretend that historical learning data is being recorded.
It should emit a real system error and enter a degraded state according to your existing resilience/recovery architecture.

25.1 Agent package structure

Create:

aariya/
├── agents/
│   ├── installed/

│   │       └── ...
│   │

The <real-agent> directories should only be populated by actual agents you implement.

The discovery system doesn't invent them.

25.2 Agent manifest

Create:

civilization/agents/manifest.py

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
import json


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AgentManifest:

    agent_id: str
    name: str
    version: str
    description: str
    entrypoint: str
    capabilities: tuple[str, ...]
    dependencies: tuple[str, ...]
    permissions: tuple[str, ...]


def load_manifest(path: Path) -> AgentManifest:

    with path.open(
        "r",
        encoding="utf-8",
    ) as file:

        data = json.load(file)

    required = {
        "agent_id",
        "name",
        "version",
        "description",
        "entrypoint",
        "capabilities",
        "dependencies",
        "permissions",
    }

    missing = required.difference(data)

    if missing:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Manifest {path} missing fields: "
            f"{sorted(missing)}"
        )

    return AgentManifest(
        agent_id=data["agent_id"],
        name=data["name"],
        version=data["version"],
        description=data["description"],
        entrypoint=data["entrypoint"],
        capabilities=tuple(data["capabilities"]),
        dependencies=tuple(data["dependencies"]),
        permissions=tuple(data["permissions"]),
    )

The manifest is metadata, not simulated runtime information.

25.3 Example of an actual agent manifest

Once you have a real agent implementation, its directory can contain:

manifest.json

{
  "agent_id": "research.agent",
  "name": "Research Agent",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Performs research using available research capabilities.",
  "entrypoint": "aariya.agents.research:ResearchAgent",
  "capabilities": [
    "web_research"
  ],
  "dependencies": [],
  "permissions": [
    "network.read",
    "knowledge.read",
    "knowledge.write"
  ]
}

Don't copy this into your system as a fake agent just for testing.

It should exist only when ResearchAgent actually exists.

25.4 Discovery engine

Create:

civilization/agents/discovery.py

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from pathlib import Path

from .manifest import AgentManifest, load_manifest


logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class AgentDiscovery:

    def __init__(
        self,
        root: Path,
    ) -> None:

        self.root = root

    def discover(self) -> list[AgentManifest]:

        if not self.root.exists():
            logger.warning(
                "Agent directory does not exist: %s",
                self.root,
            )
            return []

        manifests: list[AgentManifest] = []

        for manifest_path in self.root.rglob(
            "manifest.json"
        ):

            try:

                manifest = load_manifest(
                    manifest_path
                )

                manifests.append(manifest)

            except Exception:
                logger.exception(
                    "Invalid agent manifest: %s",
                    manifest_path,
                )

        return manifests

Now Aariya can discover agents without knowing their names beforehand.

25.5 Entrypoint loader

The manifest tells us:

aariya.agents.research:ResearchAgent

We need to load that dynamically.

Create:

civilization/agents/loader.py

from __future__ import annotations

import importlib

from .manifest import AgentManifest


def load_agent_class(
    manifest: AgentManifest,
):

    module_name, class_name = (
        manifest.entrypoint.split(":", 1)
    )

    module = importlib.import_module(
        module_name
    )

    agent_class = getattr(
        module,
        class_name,
    )

    return agent_class

Now the system isn't coupled to specific agent classes.

25.6 Validate the agent

Don't immediately trust dynamically discovered code.

Create:

civilization/agents/validation.py

from __future__ import annotations

from .manifest import AgentManifest
from .runtime import AgentRuntime


class AgentValidator:

    def validate_manifest(
        self,
        manifest: AgentManifest,
    ) -> None:

        if not manifest.agent_id:
            raise ValueError(
                "Agent ID cannot be empty"
            )

        if not manifest.version:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{manifest.agent_id}: "
                "version missing"
            )

        if not manifest.entrypoint:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{manifest.agent_id}: "
                "entrypoint missing"
            )

    def validate_instance(
        self,
        agent: object,
    ) -> None:

        if not isinstance(
            agent,
            AgentRuntime,
        ):
            raise TypeError(
                "Loaded object does not implement "
                "AgentRuntime"
            )

This prevents arbitrary objects from entering the civilization runtime.

25.7 Dependency resolution

Agents can depend on capabilities or other infrastructure.

For example:

Research Agent
       │
       ├── web_research
       └── knowledge_memory

Create:

civilization/agents/dependencies.py

from __future__ import annotations

from .manifest import AgentManifest


class DependencyResolver:

    def __init__(
        self,
        available_capabilities: set[str],
    ) -> None:

        self.available_capabilities = (
            available_capabilities
        )

    def check(
        self,
        manifest: AgentManifest,
    ) -> list[str]:

        missing = [
            dependency
            for dependency in manifest.dependencies
            if dependency
            not in self.available_capabilities
        ]

        return missing

We aren't automatically assuming that a capability exists.

We check the real capability registry.

25.8 Discovery service

Now combine everything.

Create:

civilization/agents/discovery_service.py

from __future__ import annotations

import logging

from .discovery import AgentDiscovery
from .loader import load_agent_class
from .validation import AgentValidator
from .dependencies import DependencyResolver
from .registry import AgentRegistry


logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class AgentDiscoveryService:

    def __init__(
        self,
        discovery: AgentDiscovery,
        validator: AgentValidator,
        registry: AgentRegistry,
    ) -> None:

        self.discovery = discovery
        self.validator = validator
        self.registry = registry

    async def discover_and_register(
        self,
        available_capabilities: set[str],
    ) -> None:

        manifests = self.discovery.discover()

        resolver = DependencyResolver(
            available_capabilities
        )

        for manifest in manifests:

            try:

                self.validator.validate_manifest(
                    manifest
                )

                missing = resolver.check(
                    manifest
                )

                if missing:

                    logger.warning(
                        "Agent %s has missing "
                        "dependencies: %s",
                        manifest.agent_id,
                        missing,
                    )

                    continue

                agent_class = load_agent_class(
                    manifest
                )

                agent = agent_class()

                self.validator.validate_instance(
                    agent
                )

                await self.registry.register(
                    agent
                )

                logger.info(
                    "Agent registered: %s",
                    manifest.agent_id,
                )

            except Exception:

                logger.exception(
                    "Failed to load agent: %s",
                    manifest.agent_id,
                )

Now discovery is dynamic.

25.9 Don't automatically start every discovered agent

This is an important architectural distinction.

Discovery ≠ activation.

When Aariya starts:

DISCOVERED
    ↓
VALIDATED
    ↓
AVAILABLE

not:

DISCOVERED
    ↓
ACTIVE

Otherwise your resource-management system defeats itself.

The Governor decides when activation is necessary.

Extend agent.py:

from sqlalchemy import Boolean


class AgentRecord(Base):

    __tablename__ = "agents"

    agent_id: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(255),
        primary_key=True,
    )

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(

This gives us a distinction between:

Installed
Enabled
Available

These are not the same thing.

25.15 One more thing: agent heartbeats

An agent can be registered but dead.

So every active agent needs a heartbeat.

Conceptually:

Agent
  │
  ├── state
  ├── health
  ├── last heartbeat
  └── workload

Add:

class AgentHeartbeat(Base):

    __tablename__ = "agent_heartbeats"

    agent_id: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(255),
        primary_key=True,
    )

    timestamp: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
    )

    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(64),
        nullable=False,
    )

The Governor can then distinguish:

ACTIVE + heartbeat recent

from:

ACTIVE + heartbeat stale

The second one should become:

DEGRADED

and eventually:

FAILED

depending on actual recovery behavior.

25.16 Important: don't use arbitrary heartbeat timeouts yet

The correct architecture is:

       +

       +

We'll build that properly later.

26.1 Capability lifecycle

Capabilities need their own lifecycle.

DISCOVERED
    │
    ▼
VALIDATING
    │
    ▼
AVAILABLE
    │
    ▼
LOADED
    │
    ▼
ACTIVE
    │
    ▼
IDLE
    │
    ▼
UNLOADED
    │
    ▼
DISABLED
    │
    ▼
REMOVED

And if something goes wrong:

ACTIVE
  │
  ▼
FAILED
  │
  ▼
QUARANTINED

This is independent of the agent lifecycle.

26.2 Capability runtime contract

Create:

civilization/capabilities/runtime.py
from __future__ import annotations

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from typing import Any

from .state import CapabilityState


class CapabilityRuntime(ABC):

    @property
    @abstractmethod
    def capability_id(self) -> str:
        ...

    @property
    @abstractmethod
    def state(self) -> CapabilityState:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def load(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def unload(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def health(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def execute(
        self,
        request: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        ...

This becomes the universal interface.

A web capability, database capability, speech capability, vision capability, etc. can all use the same runtime contract.

26.3 Capability states

Create:

civilization/capabilities/state.py
from enum import Enum


class CapabilityState(str, Enum):

    DISCOVERED = "discovered"
    VALIDATING = "validating"
    AVAILABLE = "available"
    LOADED = "loaded"
    ACTIVE = "active"
    IDLE = "idle"
    UNLOADED = "unloaded"
    DISABLED = "disabled"
    FAILED = "failed"
    QUARANTINED = "quarantined"
    REMOVED = "removed"
26.4 Improve the capability manifest

The earlier manifest needs more information.

civilization/capabilities/manifest.py
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
import json


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CapabilityManifest:

    capability_id: str
    name: str
    version: str
    description: str

    entrypoint: str

    permissions: tuple[str, ...]
    dependencies: tuple[str, ...]

    input_schema: dict
    output_schema: dict


def load_manifest(
    path: Path,
) -> CapabilityManifest:

    with path.open(
        "r",
        encoding="utf-8",
    ) as file:

        data = json.load(file)

    required = {
        "capability_id",
        "name",
        "version",
        "description",
        "entrypoint",
        "permissions",
        "dependencies",
        "input_schema",
        "output_schema",
    }

    missing = required - data.keys()

    if missing:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Missing manifest fields: {sorted(missing)}"
        )

    return CapabilityManifest(
        capability_id=data["capability_id"],
        name=data["name"],
        version=data["version"],
        description=data["description"],
        entrypoint=data["entrypoint"],
        permissions=tuple(data["permissions"]),
        dependencies=tuple(data["dependencies"]),
        input_schema=data["input_schema"],
        output_schema=data["output_schema"],
    )
26.5 Why input/output schemas matter

An agent shouldn't need to know implementation details.

For example:

Capability:

web_research

INPUT

query: string
max_sources: integer

OUTPUT

sources: array
claims: array
provenance: object

Then an agent can simply ask:

execute(
    capability="web_research",
    request={
        "query": "...",
        "max_sources": 10
    }
)

It doesn't care whether the capability internally uses:

an API
browser automation
a search provider
another service

That abstraction is extremely valuable.

26.6 Capability loader

Create:

civilization/capabilities/loader.py
from __future__ import annotations

import importlib

from .manifest import CapabilityManifest


def load_capability_class(
    manifest: CapabilityManifest,
):

    module_name, class_name = (
        manifest.entrypoint.split(":", 1)
    )

    module = importlib.import_module(
        module_name
    )

    capability_class = getattr(
        module,
        class_name,
    )

    return capability_class

Again, no hardcoded capability classes.

26.7 Capability registry

Replace the simple registry with a runtime-aware registry.

civilization/capabilities/registry.py
from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio

from .runtime import CapabilityRuntime


class CapabilityRegistry:

    def __init__(self) -> None:

        self._capabilities: dict[
            str,
            CapabilityRuntime,
        ] = {}

        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def register(
        self,
        capability: CapabilityRuntime,
    ) -> None:

        async with self._lock:

            if (
                capability.capability_id
                in self._capabilities
            ):
                raise ValueError(
                    "Capability already registered: "
                    f"{capability.capability_id}"
                )

            self._capabilities[
                capability.capability_id
            ] = capability

    async def unregister(
        self,
        capability_id: str,
    ) -> None:

        async with self._lock:

            self._capabilities.pop(
                capability_id,
                None,
            )

    async def get(
        self,
        capability_id: str,
    ) -> CapabilityRuntime | None:

        async with self._lock:
            return self._capabilities.get(
                capability_id
            )

    async def all(
        self,
    ) -> list[CapabilityRuntime]:

        async with self._lock:
            return list(
                self._capabilities.values()
            )
26.8 Dynamic capability discovery

Create:

civilization/capabilities/discovery.py
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from pathlib import Path

from .manifest import (
    CapabilityManifest,
    load_manifest,
)


logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class CapabilityDiscovery:

    def __init__(
        self,
        root: Path,
    ) -> None:

        self.root = root

    def discover(
        self,
    ) -> list[CapabilityManifest]:

        if not self.root.exists():

            logger.warning(
                "Capability directory does not exist: %s",
                self.root,
            )

            return []

        manifests = []

        for path in self.root.rglob(
            "manifest.json"
        ):

            try:

                manifests.append(
                    load_manifest(path)
                )

            except Exception:

                logger.exception(
                    "Invalid capability manifest: %s",
                    path,
                )

        return manifests

Now Aariya doesn't need:

capabilities = [
    WebSearch(),
    Python(),
    Database(),
]

The filesystem/package environment is the source of truth.

26.9 Capability validation

Create:

civilization/capabilities/validation.py
from __future__ import annotations

from .manifest import CapabilityManifest
from .runtime import CapabilityRuntime


class CapabilityValidator:

    def validate_manifest(
        self,
        manifest: CapabilityManifest,
    ) -> None:

        if not manifest.capability_id:
            raise ValueError(
                "Capability ID is empty"
            )

        if not manifest.version:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{manifest.capability_id}: "
                "version is required"
            )

        if ":" not in manifest.entrypoint:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{manifest.capability_id}: "
                "invalid entrypoint"
            )

    def validate_runtime(
        self,
        capability: object,
    ) -> None:

        if not isinstance(
            capability,
            CapabilityRuntime,
        ):
            raise TypeError(
                "Capability does not implement "
                "CapabilityRuntime"
            )
26.10 Permission model

This is one of the most important additions.

A capability shouldn't automatically receive unrestricted access.

Example:

web_research

    compute.execute

    filesystem.read

    notification.send

An agent might request:

agent
  ↓

  ↓

The permission manager decides whether it's allowed.

26.11 Permission checker

Create:

civilization/security/permissions.py
from __future__ import annotations


class PermissionManager:

    def __init__(
        self,
        granted_permissions: dict[
            str,
            set[str],
        ],
    ) -> None:

        self.granted_permissions = (
            granted_permissions
        )

    def check(
        self,
        agent_id: str,
        required: set[str],
    ) -> bool:

        granted = self.granted_permissions.get(
            agent_id,
            set(),
        )

        return required.issubset(granted)

Later we'll replace static permission configuration with your existing security/policy system.

26.12 Capability acquisition

Now an agent shouldn't directly import capabilities.

Create:

civilization/capabilities/acquisition.py
from __future__ import annotations

from .registry import CapabilityRegistry


class CapabilityAcquisition:

    def __init__(
        self,
        registry: CapabilityRegistry,
    ) -> None:

        self.registry = registry

    async def acquire(
        self,
        capability_id: str,
    ):

        capability = await self.registry.get(
            capability_id
        )

        if capability is None:
            raise LookupError(
                f"Capability unavailable: "
                f"{capability_id}"
            )

        return capability

This is the abstraction boundary.

26.18 Capability execution wrapper

Create:

civilization/capabilities/executor.py
from __future__ import annotations

import time


class CapabilityExecutor:

    async def execute(
        self,
        capability,
        request: dict,
    ):

        started = time.perf_counter()

        success = False
        result = None

        try:

            result = await capability.execute(
                request
            )

            success = True

            return result

        finally:

            elapsed_ms = (
                time.perf_counter()
                - started
            ) * 1000

            # This is REAL measured execution time.
            # Send it to the telemetry repository.
            await self.record_execution(
                capability_id=capability.capability_id,
                success=success,
                latency_ms=elapsed_ms,
            )

    async def record_execution(
        self,
        capability_id: str,
        success: bool,
        latency_ms: float,
    ) -> None:

        # Connect this to the existing PostgreSQL
        # telemetry repository.
        raise NotImplementedError

One thing here needs changing before production:

Don't leave record_execution() as NotImplementedError in the actual running path.

Connect it directly to the PostgreSQL repository when integrating this milestone.

I'm showing the separation because execution and persistence shouldn't become one giant class.

27.5 Capability matcher

Now we can find agents capable of fulfilling those requirements.

Create:

matcher.py

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

from ..agents.registry import AgentRegistry
from ..capabilities.registry import CapabilityRegistry
from .requirements import TaskRequirements


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AgentCandidate:

    agent_id: str
    capabilities: frozenset[str]
    missing_capabilities: frozenset[str]
    state: str


class AgentMatcher:

    def __init__(
        self,
        agent_registry: AgentRegistry,
        capability_registry: CapabilityRegistry,
    ) -> None:

        self.agent_registry = agent_registry
        self.capability_registry = capability_registry

    async def find_candidates(
        self,
        requirements: TaskRequirements,
    ) -> list[AgentCandidate]:

        agents = await self.agent_registry.all()

        candidates: list[AgentCandidate] = []

        for agent in agents:

            agent_capabilities = frozenset(
                getattr(
                    agent,
                    "capabilities",
                    (),
                )
            )

            missing = (
                requirements.capabilities
                - agent_capabilities
            )

            candidates.append(
                AgentCandidate(
                    agent_id=agent.agent_id,
                    capabilities=agent_capabilities,
                    missing_capabilities=frozenset(
                        missing
                    ),
                    state=agent.state.value,
                )
            )

        return candidates

One thing is intentionally missing:

No fabricated ranking.

At this point we simply establish compatibility.

27.6 Better matching through the Capability Registry

An agent might not directly expose every capability.

So the matcher should eventually resolve:

Agent
 ↓
Declared capabilities
 ↓
Capability registry
 ↓
Dependency graph
 ↓
Available execution paths

For now add:

async def available_capabilities(
    registry: CapabilityRegistry,
) -> set[str]:

    capabilities = await registry.all()

    return {
        capability.capability_id
        for capability in capabilities
    }

Then:

available = await available_capabilities(
    self.capability_registry
)

Now the system knows what is actually installed.

27.7 Don't confuse installed with usable

A capability can be:

INSTALLED
AVAILABLE
LOADED
ACTIVE
FAILED
DISABLED
QUARANTINED

Therefore:

capability.state

must be checked.

Only capabilities in an appropriate operational state should participate in planning.

27.8 Execution plan

Create:

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

from .requirements import TaskRequirements


@dataclass
class ExecutionPlan:

    task_id: str

    agent_ids: list[str] = field(
        default_factory=list

        default_factory=list

    blocked_reasons: list[str] = field(

27.9 Planner — first safe implementation
from __future__ import annotations

from .matcher import AgentCandidate
from .models import Task
from .requirements import TaskRequirements
from .planner import ExecutionPlan


class TaskPlanner:

    def plan(
        self,
        task: Task,
        requirements: TaskRequirements,
        candidates: list[AgentCandidate],
    ) -> ExecutionPlan:

        plan = ExecutionPlan(
            task_id=task.task_id,
        )

        for candidate in candidates:

            if candidate.missing_capabilities:
                continue

            if candidate.state in {
                "failed",
                "quarantined",
                "terminated",
            }:
                continue

            plan.agent_ids.append(
                candidate.agent_id
            )

        plan.capabilities.extend(
            requirements.capabilities
        )

        if not plan.agent_ids:

            plan.blocked_reasons.append(
                "No currently available agent "
                "satisfies the required capabilities."
            )

        return plan

This is deliberately conservative.

We're not yet saying:

"Agent A is 93% better than Agent B."

because we haven't collected enough real historical evidence.

27.10 The historical intelligence layer

Now we use the telemetry we've built.

Suppose Aariya has actually executed:

research.agent
    142 tasks
    136 successful

analysis.agent
    57 tasks
    51 successful

Those numbers come from PostgreSQL.

Never:

research_score = 0.95

That would violate your requirement.

27.11 Query real history

Create:

persistence/repositories/agent_history.py

from __future__ import annotations

from sqlalchemy import select, func
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from ..models.task import TaskExecution


async def get_agent_execution_history(
    session: AsyncSession,
    agent_id: str,
) -> dict[str, int]:

    result = await session.execute(
        select(
            TaskExecution.status,
            func.count(TaskExecution.id),
        )
        .where(
            TaskExecution.agent_id == agent_id
        )
        .group_by(
            TaskExecution.status
        )
    )

    return {
        status: count
        for status, count in result.all()
    }

Now the Governor can obtain actual historical performance.

27.12 Calculate historical reliability

This is derived from actual data:

def calculate_reliability(
    history: dict[str, int],
) -> float | None:

    completed = history.get(
        "completed",
        0,
    )

    failed = history.get(
        "failed",
        0,
    )

    total = completed + failed

    if total == 0:
        return None

    return completed / total

Notice:

no historical data
        ↓
None

not:

0.5

and not:

0.95

We never fabricate a prior performance level.

27.13 This creates an important distinction

An agent with no history is:

UNKNOWN

not:

and not:

GOOD

So candidate evidence can be:

Recent failures: actual DB measurement

versus:

That is honest intelligence.

27.19 Now add the Agent Activation Controller

The planner produces:

Agent A
Agent B

The lifecycle manager actually activates them.

Create:

civilization/tasks/activation.py

from __future__ import annotations

from ..agents.registry import AgentRegistry
from ..agents.state import AgentState


class AgentActivationController:

    def __init__(
        self,
        registry: AgentRegistry,
    ) -> None:

        self.registry = registry

    async def activate(
        self,
        agent_ids: list[str],
    ) -> None:

        for agent_id in agent_ids:

            agent = await self.registry.get(
                agent_id
            )

            if agent is None:
                raise LookupError(
                    f"Agent unavailable: {agent_id}"
                )

            if agent.state == AgentState.ACTIVE:
                continue

            if agent.state in {
                AgentState.SUSPENDED,
                AgentState.IDLE,
                AgentState.AVAILABLE,
            }:

                await agent.resume()

This is where the actual runtime changes state.

from __future__ import annotations

from datetime import datetime

from sqlalchemy import (
    BigInteger,
    DateTime,
    String,
    Text,
)
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import JSONB
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from ..database import Base


class GovernorDecision(Base):

    __tablename__ = "governor_decisions"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        BigInteger,
        primary_key=True,
        autoincrement=True,
    )

    timestamp: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
        index=True,
    )

    task_id: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(255),
        nullable=False,
        index=True,
    )

    decision_type: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(100),
        nullable=False,
    )

    decision: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
        JSONB,
        nullable=False,
    )

    evidence: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
        JSONB,
        nullable=False,
    )

    reason: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        Text,
        nullable=False,
    )

Now Aariya can later learn:

Decision
 ↓
What evidence existed?
 ↓
What did Governor do?
 ↓
What happened?

That is the basis of your autonomous learning layer.

27.26 Very important: don't let the learning system modify decisions yet

At this milestone:

Historical data
        ↓
Decision support

Not:

Historical data
        ↓
self-modifying policy

We need enough real observations first.

Otherwise the system could learn from:

insufficient data
one-off failures
measurement errors
unusual workloads

and then amplify those mistakes.

27.27 Add a confidence state

The planner should distinguish:

HIGH EVIDENCE
MEDIUM EVIDENCE
LOW EVIDENCE
UNKNOWN

But don't assign arbitrary numerical confidence.

For example:

historical executions = 0

means:

evidence = UNKNOWN

while:

historical executions = 500

provides more evidence.

Later, the statistical evaluation layer can determine confidence properly.

Milestone 28 — Dynamic Agent Lifecycle & Resource Governor

This is the milestone where Aariya's Governor becomes an actual resource manager.

The goal is:

Observe what is really happening → understand what is needed → activate only necessary agents → keep useful agents alive → put unnecessary agents idle → reclaim resources → recover agents when demand returns.

And we will keep your rule throughout:

No mock data. No synthetic telemetry. No fake agents. No hardcoded runtime measurements.

28.1 The architecture
                         AARIYA
                            │
                            ▼
                       GOVERNOR
                            │
             ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
             ▼              ▼              ▼
       TASK OBSERVER   AGENT OBSERVER   RESOURCE OBSERVER
             │              │              │

The important design decision:

The Governor does not directly kill processes.

It tells the Lifecycle Manager what transition should occur.

Governor

This gives us a safety boundary.

28.2 Agent lifecycle states

If you haven't already created this, use:

civilization/agents/state.py
from enum import Enum


class AgentState(str, Enum):

    DISCOVERED = "discovered"

    VALIDATING = "validating"

    AVAILABLE = "available"

    STARTING = "starting"

    ACTIVE = "active"

    IDLE = "idle"

    SUSPENDING = "suspending"

    SUSPENDED = "suspended"

    STOPPING = "stopping"

    TERMINATED = "terminated"

    DEGRADED = "degraded"

    FAILED = "failed"

    QUARANTINED = "quarantined"

Don't collapse IDLE and SUSPENDED.

They mean different things.

IDLE

The agent remains loaded and can respond quickly.

SUSPENDED

The agent's runtime resources have been released as much as possible.

28.3 Why this distinction matters

Imagine:

Research Agent

It hasn't received work for 20 seconds.

Putting it immediately into SUSPENDED could actually make things worse if another research task arrives 2 seconds later.

So:

ACTIVE
  ↓
IDLE
  ↓
SUSPENDED

should normally happen progressively.

Not:

ACTIVE → KILL
28.4 Create the agent runtime contract

Your agents need lifecycle methods.

civilization/agents/runtime.py
from __future__ import annotations

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from typing import Any

from .state import AgentState


class AgentRuntime(ABC):

    @property
    @abstractmethod
    def agent_id(self) -> str:
        ...

    @property
    @abstractmethod
    def state(self) -> AgentState:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def start(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def pause(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def resume(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def stop(self) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def health(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def execute(
        self,
        request: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        ...
28.5 The Governor needs a snapshot

Don't let the Governor query ten different services independently during every decision.

Create one runtime snapshot.

28.9 Resource observer

Use the OS itself.

For Linux/macOS:

import psutil


def collect_resource_snapshot() -> ResourceSnapshot:

    memory = psutil.virtual_memory()

    load = psutil.getloadavg()

    return ResourceSnapshot(
        timestamp=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        cpu_percent=psutil.cpu_percent(
            interval=None
        ),
        memory_percent=memory.percent,
        available_memory_bytes=memory.available,
        load_average=load[0],
    )

This is real machine telemetry.

Install:

pip install psutil

Don't feed it fabricated measurements.

28.10 Why interval=None?

Because the Governor should not block while collecting CPU information.

The monitoring system can continuously maintain measurements.

Later we'll improve this with a dedicated telemetry loop.

28.11 Task pressure

Now calculate actual workload.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class WorkloadState:

    queued: int
    running: int
    waiting: int

And derive it from PostgreSQL.

For example:

from sqlalchemy import select, func


async def get_task_counts(
    session,
) -> WorkloadState:

    result = await session.execute(
        select(
            TaskExecution.status,
            func.count(TaskExecution.id),
        )
        .group_by(TaskExecution.status)
    )

    counts = dict(result.all())

    return WorkloadState(
        queued=counts.get("queued", 0),
        running=counts.get("running", 0),
        waiting=counts.get("waiting", 0),
    )

This is real workload.

28.12 Agent activity

For each agent:

active tasks
queued tasks
last execution
last heartbeat
historical executions
recent failures

The Governor should get those from the actual agent repository.

Don't maintain a second fake in-memory truth.

28.13 Decision types

Create:

from enum import Enum


class GovernorAction(str, Enum):

    KEEP_ACTIVE = "keep_active"

    ACTIVATE = "activate"

    KEEP_IDLE = "keep_idle"

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

The evidence is important.

Aariya should be able to explain:

Why did you suspend this agent?

with actual observations.

28.15 Don't create arbitrary thresholds everywhere

Avoid this architecture:

if cpu > 80:
    suspend()

That is too primitive.

Instead, the Governor should examine:

Agent demand
+
task queue
+
agent dependencies
+
resource pressure
+
recent utilization
+
expected near-term workload
+
startup/resume cost
+
historical usefulness

Some of these values are already available.

Others we'll build in subsequent milestones.

28.16 First lifecycle policy

We can safely implement a conservative policy now.

class LifecyclePolicy:

    def decide(
        self,
        agent: AgentSnapshot,
        workload: WorkloadState,
        resources: ResourceSnapshot,
    ) -> GovernorDecision:

        if agent.state == "failed":

            return GovernorDecision(
                agent_id=agent.agent_id,
                action=GovernorAction.RECOVER,
                reasons=(
                    "Agent is in failed state.",
                ),
                evidence={
                    "state": agent.state,
                },
            )

        if agent.active_tasks > 0:

            return GovernorDecision(
                agent_id=agent.agent_id,
                action=GovernorAction.KEEP_ACTIVE,
                reasons=(
                    "Agent currently has active work.",
                ),
                evidence={
                    "active_tasks":
                        agent.active_tasks,
                },
            )

        if agent.queued_tasks > 0:

            return GovernorDecision(
                agent_id=agent.agent_id,
                action=GovernorAction.RESUME,
                reasons=(
                    "Agent has queued work.",
                ),
                evidence={
                    "queued_tasks":
                        agent.queued_tasks,
                },
            )

        if agent.state == "active":

            return GovernorDecision(
                agent_id=agent.agent_id,
                action=GovernorAction.KEEP_IDLE,
                reasons=(
                    "Agent has no currently "
                    "assigned work.",
                ),
                evidence={
                    "active_tasks":
                        agent.active_tasks,
                        "queued_tasks":
                        agent.queued_tasks,
                },
            )

        return GovernorDecision(
            agent_id=agent.agent_id,
            action=GovernorAction.NO_ACTION,
            reasons=(
                "No lifecycle transition "
                "required from current evidence.",
            ),
            evidence={
                "state": agent.state,
            },
        )

Notice what we're not doing.

We are not saying:

idle for 30 sec
→ suspend

yet.

That needs real historical workload behavior.

28.17 Why?

Suppose actual data shows:

Research Agent:

10:00 active
10:01 idle
10:02 active
10:03 idle
10:04 active

Suspending it every minute would waste resources due to constant startup/resume operations.

Another agent might show:

10:00 active
10:01 idle
10:02 idle
10:03 idle
10:04 idle
10:05 idle

That agent is a much better suspension candidate.

We need the system to learn this from actual history.

28.18 Add lifecycle history

Create:

agent_lifecycle_events

with:

agent_id
